messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Electronic Health Record Discharge Summary: Hispanic Male with Diabetes Mellitus Type 2 and Sepsis

Identification: 
Patient: 42-year-old Hispanic male with a history of diabetes mellitus type 2 
Admitted: Emergency department admission on September 1, 2017 for sepsis 

Hospital Course: 
The patient had a six-day history of malaise, headache, fever, and generalized body pain. He had developed diarrhea, tachypnea, and confusion three days prior to admission. On the day of admission, he became drowsy, dyspneic, and looked very ill. Physical examination showed the patient was severely dehydrated with a blood pressure of 60/30 mmHg and respiratory rate of 32 bpm. 
Treatment with intravenous fluids, antibiotics, insulin, and other supportive therapies was administered. Methimazole, hydrocortisone, and Lugol's solution were added on the second day of treatment. On the third day of treatment, there was a good evolution and the patient was discontinued from norepinephrine and insulin infusion. 
ECG was normal but echocardiography showed severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Intravenous furosemide was administered for two days for acute lung edema. 
The patient continued to improve and was discharged on September 7, 2017 with almost complete recovery. 
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Follow-Up: 
Follow-up echocardiography showed complete resolution of left ventricular systolic dysfunction. After the patient was discharged, no additional study was performed.

Signatures: 
This discharge summary was reviewed and approved by (physician's name).

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The condition chiefly responsible is a thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis), shown by the methimazole, hydrocortisone and Lugol's solution, with shock, confusion and reversible cardiomyopathy alongside likely diabetic decompensation. It belongs to chapter E (endocrine diseases). Thyrotoxicosis with crisis is category E05, though diabetic ketoacidosis (E11) is a reasonable alternative because the diagnosis section is withheld and the insulin infusion suggests ketoacidosis.

CODE: E05
